newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe wins unenthusiastic confidence vote.
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe wins unenthusiastic confidence vote.

text.p: Prime Minister Alain Juppe won an unenthusiastic vote of confidence on Wednesday from a parliament sceptical about his predictions that France was poised for an economic upturn after an austerity cure.

Members of the National Assembly, where Juppe's centre-right coalition controls four-fifths of the seats, voted by 464 to 100 to endorse the premier's policies after he outlined plans for "new democracy" for the year 2000 and a drive to fight unemployment. There were four abstentions.

"I believe perseverance will pay off and that 1997 will be a year of improvement," the premier told parliament in a policy speech before the vote, urging his allies to combat gloom and convince voters the government was on the right track.

Almost all of Juppe's coalition allies voted for him while the Socialists and Communists voted against. The outcome of the vote had been a foregone conclusion and masked deep misgivings within the coalition about government austerity policies.

Juppe rejected criticisms that the vote, the third he has called and won since taking power in May 1995, was to stifle grumbling in his coalition before legislative elections in 1998. "This vote of confidence will not be a blank cheque," he said.

He said his two main priorities for coming months were "to complete, reinforce, energise our strategy for jobs" and "build a new democracy for the citizen of the year 2000" with as yet ill-defined plans to reform the state and the justice system.

Gilles de Robien, floor leader of the centrist Union for French Democracy (UDF), the junior coalition partner alongside Juppe's Juppe's conservative Rally for the Republic (RPR) party, pointedly said before the vote:
"Yes, Mr Prime Minister, you have the confidence of the UDF. In parallel, can you tell us if we, the parliamentarians of the UDF, have yours?"
He pleaded for more consultation with the UDF, and reiterated "reservations" about Juppe's suggestions to reform voting laws and a plan to tighten anti-racism laws.
Other deputies, who spoke on condition of anonymity, were more critical. "It was all so uninspiring," said one RPR deputy. "I'm disappointed," said one UDF deputy.
The opposition Socialist party said Juppe had tried to cow his allies into submission and that France needed a radical shift in policy to bolster economic growth and create jobs.
"We know France needs a change of policy. From now on, everyone will know that to change policy, we must change coalition," said former Socialist prime minister Laurent Fabius.
Juppe said a rise in unemployment to 12.6 percent of the workforce was "unacceptable". He said he would launch a "new decentralised plan of action for jobs, notably for the young".
In a 30-minute speech, he said the draft 1997 budget would bring public spending under control and put France on target to qualify for a single European Union currency from 1999.
Juppe's approval rating is near to an all-time low at 30 percent and President Jacques Chirac had to intervene twice in the last week to shield him from criticism within the coalition.
Juppe said the government would put to parliament soon a bill toughening anti-racism laws to combat "an increase in racist, anti-Semitic and xenophobic speech and behaviour".
But he hinted he might allow coalition deputies a free vote on the bill, largely aimed at countering extreme-right National Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen.
